title: Report says 'circular financing' shows AI bubble 'primed to pop'
content:
Report - Brace for Impact: Protecting People and the Economy When the AI Bubble Bursts
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom represents one of the largest speculative frenzies in history. The ten most valuable U.S. companies are all tech giants. And most U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX — are at the center of a multi-trillion-dollar spending spree on data centers and related infrastructure to train and run generative AI models. With tech companies spending drastically more on AI infrastructure than they are earning from selling AI products and services, however, even the biggest AI companies have begun borrowing heavily to cover AI’s extraordinarily high costs.
That skyrocketing debt means that AI giants will need to earn multiples more in revenue than they are earning now to cover their spending. If the AI industry can’t pay back its mounting debts, a financial crash could follow — and it could spread well beyond the tech sector.
Speculative data center debt is being repackaged and sold to pension and retirement funds, university endowments, and other institutional investors in a manner eerily reminiscent of the subprime bubble. Private equity firms have purchased life insurers and loaded them with risky debt, exposing policyholders and the public to losses and raising the threat of financial contagion.
Rather than address these mounting risks, the Trump administration and federal financial regulators are ripping up regulatory guardrails and exacerbating the harms a potential crisis would cause. They must dramatically reverse course to reduce the likelihood of disaster. Regulators, Congress, and state policymakers should instead act swiftly to shine a light on the AI industry’s murky finances, stop contributing to the inflation of the bubble with subsidies and regulatory giveaways, better protect working people’s retirement savings from outsized risk exposure, and strengthen the resilience of the financial system to protect households’ economic security and the broader economy’s stability.
This report’s purpose is not to predict a specific sequence of events or portray an economic crisis as inevitable. It is instead to argue that the ingredients for a serious crisis are in place, explain why inaction regarding the growing risks would be a dangerous mistake, and describe the steps that policymakers should take to mitigate the growing threats to economic stability. Time is running short.

report.summary: A new Open Markets Institute report warns that debt-fueled AI infrastructure spending and circular financing have inflated a speculative bubble that could burst and spread beyond tech.
report.background: The AI boom has become one of the largest speculative frenzies in history. The ten most valuable U.S. companies are tech giants, and firms including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and SpaceX are spending trillions on data centers and infrastructure to train and run generative AI. Because infrastructure spending far exceeds AI product revenue, even major companies are borrowing heavily. Data-center debt is being repackaged and sold to pension funds, endowments and insurers, echoing subprime-style risk. Meanwhile, regulators are weakening guardrails, according to the report. The report does not predict a specific crash timeline, but argues the ingredients for a serious crisis are in place and that inaction is dangerous.
key_points: AI infrastructure spending is outrunning revenue. Tech giants are building multi-trillion-dollar data-center capacity, but earnings from AI products and services are far smaller, forcing heavy borrowing. To repay debt, the industry would need revenue to grow by multiples, not incremental amounts.

Circular financing is a red flag. The report points to AI firms funding customers or one another, which can make demand look stronger than it really is. When the same money circulates through the ecosystem, reported growth can mask fragile underlying economics.

Risk is being pushed into ordinary savings. Data-center debt is packaged and sold to pension funds, university endowments and insurers, similar to subprime securitization. Private-equity-owned insurers add another channel for losses to reach policyholders and the public.

Policy is moving the wrong way. The report says the Trump administration and federal regulators are dismantling guardrails while subsidies and giveaways inflate the bubble. It urges transparency, an end to AI subsidies, protection for retirement savers and a more resilient financial system.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the warning implies tighter capital discipline: debt-funded compute buildouts may slow, weaker players could consolidate, and investors may demand clearer returns. Developers could face less cheap compute and more scrutiny of revenue claims, though open models and efficient infrastructure may benefit. Regular users may not feel it immediately, but retirement savings and insurance are exposed through securitized data-center debt; a burst could raise borrowing costs, hit jobs and investment, and cool AI product investment. The biggest risk is contagion from tech to pensions and insurers, making disclosure and regulatory oversight urgent before risks compound.
report.tools: To follow the risk: read the Open Markets Institute report; track AI capex and debt in SEC EDGAR filings; use FRED for credit and rates data; and monitor markets with OpenBB or yfinance. For open-source financial analysis, SEC EDGAR APIs and pandas-based notebooks can help compare capex, revenue and debt across AI giants.
